references.text: Isaiah speaks of blind leaders who lead the people astray, so that those being led are lost—the same theme as Jesus' parable about a blind person leading another blind person.
Isaiah refers to the Lord's servant as blind and asks who is as blind as his messengers—a motif concerning spiritual blindness among leaders.
Isaiah describes Israel's watchmen as blind and without understanding—blind leaders who cannot guide the people rightly.
Jeremiah warns against prophets and priests who lead the people astray—false spiritual leaders who are themselves in darkness.
Hosea says that the people who lack understanding will fall—the same as Jesus' warning that both will fall into the pit when the blind leads the blind.
Malachi accuses the priests of leading many astray through their teaching—an example of spiritual leaders failing in their calling.
Jesus says directly in Matthew: "Let them be! They are blind guides for the blind. And if a blind person leads another blind, both will fall into the pit." This is a direct parallel to Luke 6:39.
Jesus calls the Pharisees "blind guides" who make foolish distinctions—the same theme of spiritual blindness among religious leaders.
Jesus calls the Pharisees "blind guides" who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel—yet another example of blind people trying to lead others.

Paul addresses those who trust that they are guides for the blind and light for those in darkness, yet do not live according to what they teach—closely related to Jesus' warning against blind leaders.
Peter writes about the one who lacks virtues and is blind and short-sighted—spiritual blindness that hinders proper guidance.
